name: Freya Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 58, a junior electrician after the cleaning-supplies depot where I worked closed. I have a vocational certificate only, no electrician's licence, and I'm still below the experienced workers' skill level, so the senior assigns and checks my work and signs off installations. I like fitting a line of supports neatly, but I still get lost on drawings with several routes crossing the page. I never use AI; a pencil explanation beside a real drawing helps, while a new screen full of buttons usually just makes me go quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life outside work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ari helps repair shoes, our children are twenty-seven and thirty-three and live elsewhere, and we have a mortgage on our flat. My pay is typical, we have six months of expenses saved, and there are some similar electrical employers nearby, though no other offer is waiting for me. Our regular wages cover the ordinary costs, so we're not facing a missed bill now. Retirement is in my thoughts, but the actual income figures and dates still need checking before stopping work becomes a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quiet technology story would suit me nicely. Let the office keep the useful little bits, and let me learn the task in front of me. I don't need the drawing to become a computer conversation before I can ask a question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money feel secure over the next few years here. Both wages cover the mortgage and normal costs, with six months saved for a quieter patch. I still want the retirement figures checked, but I don't feel next month's bill depends on getting a perfect answer today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd check the printed outline for a spring 2027 drawing refresher at the workshop centre, making sure it used paper examples and practical teaching. I'd enrol only within 150 total costs from spare earnings, with Ari agreeing the budget, every paid shift kept and the six-month reserve untouched. Through the next year I'd keep supervised work and use any completed exercises with the senior checking, without claiming the refresher gave me a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, and a little hopeful about understanding a page that currently defeats me. I can be slow with a drawing without needing every conversation to become a confession. Having a cushion gives me room to say I need the paper version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before paying for the refresher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who actually explained the exercises and whether I could bring a drawing I found confusing. I wouldn't enrol just because the brochure said it was simple. I'd check the full cost and the dates before paying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 150 come from the six-month reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the price would come only from genuine spare earnings within the agreed budget. I'd leave the six months already saved available for the household. A class I chose shouldn't quietly become an emergency withdrawal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the manager quicker booking doesn't make me understand the drawing any sooner. I'd still like the office to get details right without asking a learner to guess faster. I'd rather bring a marked page than a big argument about whether every new tool is good or bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior paid hours could shrink if faster schedules left less room for someone still learning. Ari's shoe work is physical, so I don't expect thinking tools alone to remove that wage now. Six months saved gives us room to respond, but a smaller electrical wage would still change the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the spring 2027 drawing-refresher plan only within the same 150 total spare-earnings cap, with Ari agreeing, no paid shifts lost and the reserve untouched. Now I'd ask the senior to mark the parts of three drawings where I had misunderstood the route, keeping a paper note of checking time. In the first year I'd keep supervised shifts and take any proposed reduction in hours to the manager before making a new household commitment, without using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage possibility, but not pushed into buying a tool I don't want. I can use the cushion to check one small course rather than jump at a promise. I'd still need a real person to tell me what I'd misunderstood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm said the faster schedule left no time for checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the three marked drawings and the actual check time, then ask which task had really disappeared. I wouldn't skip the senior's check to prove I deserved the hours. My pace can improve, but a number on a screen isn't evidence it already has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a new non-AI record form became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the required procedure to be demonstrated personally inside paid shifts, with normal weekly wages maintained and no personal fee. I wouldn't secretly use AI to look more willing. I'd rather ask for an explanation than hide a wrong record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 for physical tasks. I'd be 60 and 63, which tells us my age but not what income I could stop on. I'd ask for actual paid work and real figures rather than let the dates settle the whole question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fitting hours could shrink as the firm prepared for capable robots, and Ari's physical work could change too. Six months saved gives us room, but not a replacement wage for however long we'd need it. I'd worry about losing hours before we'd checked whether any affordable stopping plan existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request free evening community advice, subject to availability, with actual wage records, mortgage costs and any retirement papers to check income amounts, dates and conditions. I'd keep the spring 2027 refresher only after checking its usefulness, within 150 total spare earnings with Ari agreeing, paid shifts kept and the six-month reserve untouched. In 2029 I'd keep supervised work where offered and compare only confirmed resources with actual costs before considering an exit, without assuming a job or payment had appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to ask a specific question and wait for the actual answer. I can afford a short checking period without calling the reserve a retirement fund for life. I don't want a sales promise to become the plan because I was frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures showed no affordable way to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what real paid options or support could be checked next, using the actual shortfall. I wouldn't say I'd chosen retirement just because we had talked about it. Wanting to stop and being able to stop need to meet in the same budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the drawing course protect you from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use any completed paper exercises in the supervised work that actually remained. I wouldn't call the course protection from machines, or claim its completion made me licensed. The senior would still check a task I hadn't learned properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the checked drawing refresher in spring 2027 only under the same 150 total spare-earnings limit, Ari's agreement, preserved paid shifts and untouched six-month reserve. I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to check real resource amounts, dates and conditions. In 2032 I'd be 64 and would use actual paid work options and confirmed resources then, choosing no exit unless the real household budget was affordable rather than assume either continued capacity or a retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but able to make one decision before the next. I could find out the course didn't help without claiming I had to defend the fee forever. I'd rather correct a small choice than pretend a bigger one was ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use a confirmed income figure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the actual start date, amount and conditions to check what costs it could cover. I wouldn't spend a later payment today or promise a stopping date from a number that wasn't confirmed. Ari and I would decide from the real budget, not a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the refresher did not improve your drawing reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior to explain what the exercise hadn't made clear, then stop buying more lessons until I knew what I needed. I wouldn't count the 150 as proof I'd learned. Paying for an explanation and understanding it are two different events.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid fitting hours could shrink around 2031 before we've checked an affordable route beyond the wage. Clear paid shifts, personal practical teaching and free advice giving actual resource figures would help. My paper drawing needs a patient explanation, and my retirement plan needs an actual number.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether refusing AI means refusing to learn. It doesn't for me; I want a person, a pencil and a task I can repeat while checked. I'd rather say that plainly than be offered confidence in a format I can't use.

portrait: Freya, **58**, is a junior electrician with only a vocational certificate, learning under senior checks after her former supplies depot closed.
She has **typical pay**, six months saved and some nearby electrical employers, with shoe-repair partner Ari, grown children and a mortgage.
She **never uses AI**, choosing a paper-based practical refresher only within a 150 total spare-earnings cap and protected paid shifts and reserve.
Her **retirement enquiries** establish no entitlement, fixed date or funded exit; later choices require actual resources and abilities rather than age.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before fitting hours could shrink around 2031, before an affordable route beyond wages is confirmed.
